nameStory: Ivy-leaved Duckweed gets its name from its distinctive leaf shape that resembles tiny ivy leaves, quite different from the round leaves of common duckweed. The 'duckweed' part comes from the fact that ducks and other waterfowl love to eat these tiny floating plants. It's sometimes called 'star duckweed' because multiple fronds stay connected together, creating star-like patterns in the water.
description: Ivy-leaved Duckweed is a tiny aquatic plant that floats just below the water's surface, unlike other duckweeds that float right on top. Each individual frond is only about half an inch long with a distinctive three-lobed shape that looks like a miniature ivy leaf. What makes this duckweed special is that many fronds stay connected to each other in branching chains, creating delicate underwater networks. You'll only see it floating on the surface when it's ready to flower or produce seeds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Lives underwater rather than floating on the surface like other duckweeds, forming connected chains of fronds that create lacy underwater mats

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny three-lobed fronds shaped like miniature ivy leaves, translucent green and about half an inch long with a smooth, delicate texture

idTips.label: Connection Pattern
idTips.description: Multiple fronds remain attached to each other in branching chains, unlike other duckweeds where individual plants float separately

idTips.label: Water Position
idTips.description: Fronds typically float 1-12 feet below the surface, only rising to float on top when flowering

habitat: Look for Ivy-leaved Duckweed in quiet, nutrient-rich freshwater ponds, slow streams, and shallow lake edges throughout New England. It prefers still or very slow-moving water where it can form its characteristic underwater colonies. You'll often find it mixed with other aquatic plants in areas protected from strong currents or wave action.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water warms, with fresh green fronds emerging and chains becoming more visible underwater.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when underwater colonies are most extensive. Flowering occurs now, bringing some fronds to the surface.
seasonality.fall: Fronds may begin to break apart and sink as temperatures cool, preparing to overwinter as dormant buds.
seasonality.winter: Survives as dormant winter buds (turions) on pond bottoms under ice, nearly invisible until spring growth resumes.

funFact: Ivy-leaved Duckweed is like the underwater cousin of the duckweed family - while its relatives party on the surface, it prefers to live a quiet life below, only popping up to the surface for the brief moment it needs to reproduce!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Common Duckweed, but Ivy-leaved Duckweed lives underwater (not on the surface) and has three-lobed ivy-shaped fronds instead of round ones. Memory trick: 'Ivy leaves have lobes, and this one lives low (underwater).'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'duckweed,' this plant spends most of its life completely submerged, making it quite different from what most people picture when they think of duckweed floating on pond surfaces. Many people walk right past ponds containing this species without ever noticing it below the surface.
compareHints: Unlike Common Duckweed which floats on the surface with round fronds, Ivy-leaved Duckweed lives underwater with three-lobed fronds that stay connected in chains. While Common Duckweed forms obvious green carpets on pond surfaces, you need to look into the water to spot Ivy-leaved Duckweed's translucent underwater colonies. Turion Duckweed is more similar to Common Duckweed in being surface-floating with round fronds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common duckweed differs from its relatives by having exactly one root per plant and opaque green leaves.
Turion duckweed looks almost identical to common duckweed, but produces the distinctive sinking turions that common duckweed cannot make.
